column3: The third disputed act completes the same lesson: Moses judges visible impropriety before its concealed protective purpose is disclosed.
The next episode repeats Moses's immediate condemnation of an act whose fuller rationale is withheld until later.

The teacher discloses that the acts were not done on his own command, completing the divine-authority frame behind the ship's protective defect.
What is disliked may be good while its good remains unknown; this directly parallels the harmful-looking defect that protects the vessel.

The command not to follow what one has no knowledge of supplies a direct epistemic-restraint parallel to Moses's immediate judgement.
Verification before acting on consequential information provides a broader procedural parallel to withholding judgement until grounds are known.
The warning not to press questions whose disclosure would cause distress offers a distant counterpart to the teacher's temporary prohibition on questioning.
